query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of carbon (around 0.1 at.%) to refractory high-entropy alloys can improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming stable carbides that reduce the diffusion of oxygen into the alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized refractory high-entropy alloy
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of stable carbides (e.g., Ta3C and Nb3C)
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, as the formation of stable carbides can reduce the diffusion of oxygen into the alloy, thereby improving its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxygen resistance, with a potential reduction in oxidation rate and increased service life
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 800°C to 1200°C, Pressure range: 6 GPa to 10 GPa
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of carbon required and the optimal processing conditions to achieve the desired carbide formation and improved oxygen resistance are uncertain and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose treated and untreated refractory high-entropy alloy samples to high-temperature (1000°C) and high-pressure (8 GPa) conditions for an extended period (100 hours) and measure the oxidation rate and microstructural changes.
measurements: Microstructural changes (e.g., carbide formation, grain size)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated alloy shows no significant improvement in high-temperature oxygen resistance compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
